lessons.title: Integration by Parts
lessons.description: Integrate products using the integration by parts formula.
lessons.formula:
∫u dv = uv − ∫v du

LIATE priority:
L = Logarithmic
I = Inverse trig
A = Algebraic
T = Trigonometric
E = Exponential
lessons.content:
Integration by parts is the product rule for integrals. It transforms ∫u·dv into uv−∫v·du, effectively swapping which function needs to be integrated. The LIATE rule helps choose u: pick the function type highest on the list (Logarithmic → Inverse trig → Algebraic → Trig → Exponential).

Sometimes integration by parts must be applied multiple times. The tabular method (DI method) makes repeated integration by parts faster for products of polynomials with trig or exponential functions.

Integrals like ∫ln x dx and ∫arctan x dx are solved by choosing u as the entire integrand and dv = dx.
steps: Choose u (LIATE rule) and dv = rest
Find du and v = ∫dv
Apply the formula: uv − ∫v du
Simplify and evaluate the remaining integral
If needed, apply integration by parts again

examples.title: Basic Parts
examples.text: ∫x·e^x dx. u=x, dv=e^x dx. du=dx, v=e^x. = xe^x − ∫e^x dx = xe^x − e^x + C = e^x(x−1) + C.

examples.title: Logarithm
examples.text: ∫ln x dx. u=ln x, dv=dx. du=1/x dx, v=x. = x ln x − ∫1 dx = x ln x − x + C.

lessons.tip: LIATE is your best friend for choosing u. When in doubt, pick u as the function that gets simpler when differentiated!

quiz.q: ∫x·cos x dx = ?
options: x sin x + cos x + C
x cos x − sin x + C
sin x − x cos x + C
x sin x − cos x + C
quiz.explanation: u=x, dv=cos x dx. = x sin x − ∫sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C.

quiz.q: ∫e^x · x dx. Choose u = ?
quiz.explanation: LIATE: Algebraic (x) beats Exponential (e^x). Choose u = x.

quiz.q: ∫ln(x) dx = ?
quiz.explanation: u=ln x, dv=dx. Result: x ln x − x + C.

quiz.q: LIATE stands for:
options: Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential
quiz.explanation: LIATE helps choose u: Log > Inverse trig > Algebraic > Trig > Exponential.

lessons.title: Trigonometric Integrals
lessons.description: Integrate powers of sine, cosine, and other trig functions.
lessons.formula:
sin²x = (1−cos 2x)/2
cos²x = (1+cos 2x)/2
sin x cos x = (sin 2x)/2

∫tan x dx = −ln|cos x| + C
∫sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C
lessons.content:
Trigonometric integrals involve powers and products of sin, cos, tan, and sec. The strategy depends on the powers involved. For odd powers of sin or cos, save one factor and convert the rest using Pythagorean identities.

For even powers, use half-angle formulas (power-reducing identities): sin²x = (1−cos2x)/2 and cos²x = (1+cos2x)/2. These reduce the power and make the integral manageable.

Products of sin and cos with different arguments use product-to-sum formulas.
steps: Check if the power of sin or cos is odd
If odd: save one factor, convert rest to the other trig function
If even: use half-angle formulas to reduce the power
For tan/sec integrals: use identity 1+tan²x=sec²x
Simplify and integrate

examples.title: Odd Power
examples.text: ∫sin³x dx = ∫sin²x·sin x dx = ∫(1−cos²x)·sin x dx. Let u=cos x: = cos³x/3 − cos x + C.

examples.title: Even Power
examples.text: ∫cos²x dx = ∫(1+cos 2x)/2 dx = x/2 + sin(2x)/4 + C.

lessons.tip: Odd powers are easier than even powers! With odd powers, you can 'peel off' one factor and convert the rest. Even powers always require the half-angle formula.

quiz.q: ∫sin²x dx = ?
quiz.explanation: sin²x = (1−cos 2x)/2. ∫(1−cos 2x)/2 dx = x/2 − sin(2x)/4 + C.

quiz.q: ∫cos³x dx = ?
quiz.explanation: Save one cos x: cos²x·cos x = (1−sin²x)·cos x. Let u=sin x.

quiz.q: The half-angle formula for sin²x is:
quiz.explanation: sin²x = (1−cos 2x)/2 is the half-angle (power-reducing) identity.

quiz.q: ∫tan x dx = ?
quiz.explanation: ∫sin x/cos x dx = −∫(−sin x)/cos x dx = −ln|cos x| + C.

lessons.title: Partial Fractions
lessons.description: Decompose rational functions into simpler fractions for integration.
lessons.formula:
A/(x−a) + B/(x−b) for distinct linear factors
A/(x−a) + B/(x−a)² for repeated linear factors
(Ax+B)/(x²+px+q) for irreducible quadratic factors
lessons.content:
Partial fraction decomposition breaks complex rational functions into simpler fractions that can be integrated individually. This technique applies to proper rational functions (degree of numerator < degree of denominator).

The decomposition pattern depends on the denominator factors: distinct linear factors give simple fractions, repeated factors give fractions with increasing powers, and irreducible quadratics give numerators of the form Ax+B.
steps: Factor the denominator completely
Set up the partial fraction decomposition
Multiply both sides by the denominator
Solve for the unknown coefficients A, B, C, ...
Integrate each simple fraction separately

examples.title: Repeated Factors
examples.text: ∫1/(x(x+1)²) dx = A/x + B/(x+1) + C/(x+1)². Solve for A, B, C, then integrate each term.

lessons.tip: Always factor the denominator first! The factored form tells you exactly what partial fraction form to use.

quiz.q: Partial fractions require the fraction to be:
quiz.explanation: Partial fractions work on proper rational functions. If improper, do polynomial long division first.

quiz.q: For denominator (x−1)(x+2)², the partial fraction form is:
quiz.explanation: Distinct linear factor x−1 gives A/(x−1). Repeated factor (x+2)² gives B/(x+2)+C/(x+2)².
Let u=x²+1, du=2x dx. ∫1/u du = ln|u| + C = ln(x²+1) + C.

lessons.title: Improper Integrals
lessons.description: Evaluate integrals with infinite limits or discontinuities.
lessons.formula:
Type 1 (infinite limit):
∫(a→∞) f(x)dx = lim(b→∞) ∫(a→b) f(x)dx

Type 2 (discontinuity):
∫(a→b) f(x)dx = lim(c→a⁺) ∫(c→b) f(x)dx

Converges if the limit exists (finite)
lessons.content:
Improper integrals extend definite integrals to cases with infinite limits or integrands with discontinuities. We evaluate them using limits: replace the infinite bound with a variable and take the limit.

An improper integral converges if the limit exists (is a finite number). If the limit is infinite or doesn't exist, the integral diverges. Convergence/divergence is a key concept that extends to infinite series.
steps: Identify the type: infinite limit or discontinuity
Replace the problematic bound with a variable
Evaluate the definite integral
Take the limit
If the limit is finite, the integral converges

examples.title: Infinite Upper Limit
examples.text: ∫(1→∞) 1/x² dx = lim(b→∞) [−1/x](1→b) = lim(b→∞)(−1/b+1) = 1. Converges to 1.

examples.title: Divergent Integral
examples.text: ∫(1→∞) 1/x dx = lim(b→∞) [ln x](1→b) = lim(b→∞) ln b = ∞. Diverges!

lessons.tip: Compare with the p-series: ∫(1→∞) 1/x^p converges when p > 1. This is the same rule as for p-series convergence!

quiz.explanation: lim(b→∞) ln(b) = ∞. The integral diverges.

quiz.q: An improper integral converges if:
quiz.explanation: Convergence means the limiting process gives a finite value.

lessons.title: Trigonometric Substitution
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of trigonometric substitution
lessons.formula:
Three standard substitutions:
  √(a² - x²)  →  x = a·sin(θ),  dx = a·cos(θ) dθ
  √(a² + x²)  →  x = a·tan(θ),  dx = a·sec²(θ) dθ
  √(x² - a²)  →  x = a·sec(θ),  dx = a·sec(θ)tan(θ) dθ

Key identities:
  1 - sin²(θ) = cos²(θ)
  1 + tan²(θ) = sec²(θ)
  sec²(θ) - 1 = tan²(θ)
lessons.content:
Trigonometric substitution is a technique for integrating expressions containing √(a² - x²), √(a² + x²), or √(x² - a²). The key idea is to replace x with a trig function so that the Pythagorean identities simplify the radical. After integrating with respect to θ, you convert back to x using a reference triangle.

Choose the substitution based on the form of the radical. For √(a² - x²), use x = a sin(θ), which turns the radical into a cos(θ). For √(a² + x²), use x = a tan(θ), giving the radical as a sec(θ). For √(x² - a²), use x = a sec(θ), yielding a tan(θ). Each choice is motivated by the corresponding Pythagorean identity.

After integration, draw a reference triangle to convert back from θ to x. Label the sides based on your substitution, then express sin(θ), cos(θ), tan(θ), etc. in terms of x. This is the most error-prone step — always verify your triangle is consistent with the original substitution.
steps: Identify which radical form appears: √(a²-x²), √(a²+x²), or √(x²-a²).
Make the appropriate trig substitution and compute dx in terms of dθ.
Substitute and simplify using a Pythagorean identity to eliminate the radical.
Integrate the resulting trigonometric expression with respect to θ.
Draw a reference triangle and back-substitute to express the result in terms of x.

examples.title: ∫ dx / √(4 - x²)
examples.text: Let x = 2sin(θ), dx = 2cos(θ)dθ. Radical: √(4-4sin²θ) = 2cos(θ). Integral becomes ∫ (2cosθ dθ) / (2cosθ) = ∫ dθ = θ + C. From reference triangle: sin(θ) = x/2, so θ = arcsin(x/2). Answer: arcsin(x/2) + C.

examples.title: ∫ √(25 + x²) dx
examples.text: Let x = 5tan(θ), dx = 5sec²θ dθ. Radical: √(25+25tan²θ) = 5secθ. Integral: ∫ 5secθ · 5sec²θ dθ = 25∫ sec³θ dθ. Using integration by parts on sec³: = (25/2)[secθtanθ + ln|secθ+tanθ|] + C. Back-substitute using triangle: tanθ = x/5, secθ = √(25+x²)/5.

lessons.tip: Before applying trig substitution, check if a simple u-substitution works first. For example, ∫ x/√(1-x²) dx is solved by u = 1-x². Only use trig substitution when the radical prevents a simpler approach.

quiz.q: Which substitution eliminates √(9 - x²)?
quiz.explanation: √(9 - x²) matches the form √(a²-x²) with a=3, so use x = 3sin(θ). The radical becomes 3cos(θ).

quiz.q: After substituting x = 2tan(θ), what does √(4 + x²) become?
quiz.explanation: √(4 + 4tan²θ) = √(4(1+tan²θ)) = √(4sec²θ) = 2sec(θ).

quiz.q: What identity eliminates the radical in x = 5sec(θ)?
quiz.explanation: For √(x² - a²) = √(25sec²θ - 25) = 5√(sec²θ-1) = 5|tan(θ)|, using sec² - 1 = tan².

quiz.q: The purpose of the reference triangle after integration is to:
options: Convert the answer from θ back to x
Find the value of the definite integral
quiz.explanation: After integrating in terms of θ, the reference triangle helps express trig functions of θ in terms of x.

lessons.title: Integration of Rational Functions by Partial Fractions
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of integration of rational functions by partial fractions
lessons.formula:
Partial Fraction Forms:
  Distinct linear:     A/(x-a) + B/(x-b)
  Repeated linear:     A/(x-a) + B/(x-a)² + C/(x-a)³
  Irreducible quadratic: (Ax+B)/(x²+bx+c)
  Repeated quadratic:   (Ax+B)/(x²+bx+c) + (Cx+D)/(x²+bx+c)²

After decomposition, integrate each term.
lessons.content:
Partial fraction decomposition breaks a complex rational function into simpler fractions that can be integrated individually. The method applies to proper rational functions (degree of numerator < degree of denominator). If the function is improper, first divide using polynomial long division.

The form of the decomposition depends on the denominator's factorization. For distinct linear factors (x-a)(x-b), use A/(x-a) + B/(x-b). For repeated linear factors (x-a)³, include a term for each power: A/(x-a) + B/(x-a)² + C/(x-a)³. For irreducible quadratics (x² + bx + c that has no real roots), use (Ax+B)/(x²+bx+c). Numerators of irreducible quadratic terms must be linear, not constants.

After decomposition, multiply through by the common denominator to get an identity, then solve for the coefficients by substituting strategic x-values (the cover-up method) or by equating coefficients. Each resulting term integrates to a logarithm (for linear denominators) or an arctangent plus logarithm (for irreducible quadratics).
steps: Factor the denominator completely into linear and irreducible quadratic factors.
If the degree of the numerator ≥ degree of denominator, perform polynomial long division first.
Write the partial fraction form based on the factorization.
Multiply both sides by the common denominator and solve for unknown coefficients.
Integrate each partial fraction term separately.

examples.title: ∫ 1 / (x² + 4x + 13) dx
examples.text: Complete the square: x²+4x+13 = (x+2)²+9. This is irreducible (discriminant = 16-52 < 0). ∫ 1/((x+2)²+9) dx. Substitute u = x+2, du = dx. = ∫ 1/(u²+9) du = (1/3)arctan(u/3) + C = (1/3)arctan((x+2)/3) + C.

lessons.tip: The cover-up method is a huge time-saver for distinct linear factors. To find the coefficient A for (x-a), cover up (x-a) in the original denominator and evaluate the remaining expression at x = a. This gives A directly without solving a system of equations.

quiz.q: What is the partial fraction form of 5x / ((x+1)(x-3))?
quiz.explanation: Distinct linear factors (x+1) and (x-3) give the form A/(x+1) + B/(x-3).

quiz.q: Using cover-up on (x+5)/((x-2)(x+1)), what is A for the (x-2) term?
quiz.explanation: Cover x=2 in the denominator: evaluate (2+5)/(2+1) = 7/3. So A = 7/3.

quiz.q: ∫ dx / (x² + 1) equals:
quiz.explanation: ∫ 1/(x²+1) dx = arctan(x) + C. This is a standard integral form.

quiz.q: If the denominator has (x-4)³, the partial fraction decomposition includes:
quiz.explanation: Repeated linear factors need one term for each power: A/(x-4) + B/(x-4)² + C/(x-4)³.

lessons.title: Applications: Work & Fluid Force
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of applications: work & fluid force
lessons.formula:
Work by a variable force:
  W = ∫ₐ⁶ F(x) dx

Hooke's Law:  F = kx

Hydrostatic Force:
  F = ∫ ρ·g·d(y)·L(y) dy
  ρ = fluid density, d(y) = depth, L(y) = width

Pumping Work:
  W = ∫ ρ·g·A(y)·D(y) dy
  D(y) = distance fluid is lifted
lessons.content:
In physics, work is force times displacement: W = F · d when the force is constant. When the force varies with position (like stretching a spring), we use the integral W = ∫ F(x) dx. Hooke's Law states that the spring force is F(x) = kx, where k is the spring constant and x is the displacement from equilibrium.

Fluid force (hydrostatic force) on a submerged surface depends on pressure, which increases with depth. The pressure at depth d is P = ρgd, where ρ is the fluid density and g = 9.8 m/s². The total force on a vertical plate submerged in fluid is F = ∫ₐ⁶ ρ·g·d(y)·L(y) dy, where d(y) is the depth of each horizontal strip and L(y) is the strip's width.

Pumping problems calculate the work required to pump fluid out of a tank. Each thin layer of fluid at height y must be lifted a distance D(y) to the top of the tank. The work for each layer is its weight (ρg · volume) times the lifting distance. Integrating over all layers gives the total work: W = ∫ ρ·g·A(y)·D(y) dy.
steps: Identify what varies: position (spring), depth (fluid force), or height (pumping).
Express the force or weight of a thin slice as a function of the variable.
Express the displacement or distance for that slice.
Multiply force × distance (or pressure × area) to get the integrand.
Integrate over the appropriate interval.

examples.title: Spring: 20 N force stretches spring 0.5 m. Find work to stretch 1.2 m from rest.
examples.text: Hooke's Law: F = kx → 20 = k(0.5) → k = 40 N/m. W = ∫₀¹·² 40x dx = [20x²]₀¹·² = 20(1.44) = 28.8 Joules.

examples.title: Triangular plate (base 4m, height 3m) submerged with vertex at surface, base at depth 3m
examples.text: At depth y (0 to 3), width by similar triangles: L(y) = 4y/3. Depth = y. F = ∫₀³ ρg·y·(4y/3) dy = (4ρg/3)∫₀³ y² dy = (4ρg/3)(9) = 12ρg. For water (ρg = 9800 N/m³): F = 117,600 N.

lessons.tip: For pumping problems, always draw the tank, label the water level and spout height, and write D(y) = (distance from slice to top of tank) + (spout height if applicable). The most common error is getting the distance wrong.

quiz.q: A spring has k = 200 N/m. Work to compress it 0.3 m from equilibrium is:
quiz.explanation: W = ∫₀⁰³ 200x dx = [100x²]₀⁰³ = 100(0.09) = 9 Joules.

quiz.q: Hydrostatic pressure at depth d in a fluid is:
quiz.explanation: P = ρgd, where ρ is fluid density, g is gravitational acceleration, and d is depth.

quiz.q: To pump water from a full cylindrical tank (radius 2m, height 5m) to a point 1m above:
options: Integrate from 0 to 5 with D(y) = 5 - y + 1
Integrate from 0 to 5 with D(y) = y + 1
Integrate from 0 to 6 with D(y) = y
quiz.explanation: A slice at height y (0=bottom, 5=top) must travel (5-y) to reach the top + 1m for the spout. D(y) = 5 - y + 1 = 6 - y.

quiz.q: Hooke's Law applies when the spring force is:
options: Proportional to the square of displacement
quiz.explanation: Hooke's Law: F = kx, force is directly proportional to displacement x from the equilibrium position.

lessons.title: Arc Length Parametrization
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of arc length parametrization
lessons.formula:
Arc Length of y = f(x):
  L = ∫ₐ⁶ √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx

Arc Length for parametric (x(t), y(t)):
  L = ∫ₐ⁶ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt

Arc Length Parameter:
  s(t) = ∫ₐᵗ √((dx/du)² + (dy/du)²) du
lessons.content:
The arc length of a curve is the distance you would travel if you walked along the curve from point A to point B. For a function y = f(x) on [a, b], the length is L = ∫ₐ⁶ √(1 + (f'(x))²) dx. This formula comes from approximating the curve by small line segments (the differential of arc length ds = √(1+(dy/dx)²) dx) and integrating.

For a parametric curve defined by (x(t), y(t)) on [a, b], the arc length formula uses the speed: L = ∫ₐ⁶ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt. The quantity √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) is the speed of the particle tracing the curve. The arc length parameter s(t) measures how far along the curve you have traveled from the starting point at parameter value a.

A curve is parametrized by arc length when s equals the parameter itself, meaning the speed is exactly 1 everywhere. This simplifies many formulas in differential geometry and physics, since the parameter change equals the actual distance traveled.
steps: Find the derivative: f'(x) for y=f(x), or dx/dt and dy/dt for parametric curves.
Set up the arc length integrand: √(1 + [f'(x)]²) or √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²).
Identify the interval [a, b] corresponding to the desired portion of the curve.
Evaluate the integral (often requires numerical methods or trigonometric identities).
The result L gives the total arc length in the appropriate units.

examples.title: Arc length of y = x^(3/2) from x = 0 to x = 4
Parametric: x = cos(t), y = sin(t) on [0, 2π]
examples.text: dx/dt = -sin(t), dy/dt = cos(t). √(sin²t + cos²t) = 1. L = ∫₀²π 1 dt = 2π. This confirms the circumference of the unit circle is 2π, and the speed is constant (uniform circular motion).

lessons.tip: Arc length integrals often lead to square roots that are hard to integrate symbolically. If you encounter √(1 + x⁴) or similar, you may need numerical approximation (Simpson's rule or a calculator). Don't waste time trying to find an impossible antiderivative.

quiz.q: Find the arc length of y = 2x from x = 0 to x = 3.
For a parametric curve, the speed √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) equals:
quiz.explanation: The speed is ds/dt = √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²), the rate of change of arc length with respect to the parameter.

quiz.q: A curve parametrized by arc length has speed:
quiz.explanation: If s = t (the parameter equals arc length), then ds/dt = 1 everywhere, meaning constant unit speed.

quiz.q: The arc length of the curve y = ln(cos x) from x = 0 to x = π/3 is:
quiz.explanation: dy/dx = -tan(x). L = ∫₀π/3 √(1+tan²x) dx = ∫₀π/3 sec(x) dx = [ln|sec(x)+tan(x)|]₀π/3 = ln(2+√3) - ln(1) = ln(2+√3). Hmm, actually: sec(π/3)=2, tan(π/3)=√3. So ln(2+√3) is closer to ln(3.73). Let me just state the answer is ln(2+√3).

lessons.title: Area in Polar Coordinates
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of area in polar coordinates
lessons.formula:
Area in Polar Coordinates:
  A = (1/2) ∫αᵞ [r(θ)]² dθ

Area between two curves:
  A = (1/2) ∫ [r₁(θ)]² - [r₂(θ)]² dθ

Common polar curves:
  r = a·cos(nθ): n petals if n odd, 2n if n even
lessons.content:
In polar coordinates, a point is described by (r, θ) where r is the distance from the origin and θ is the angle from the positive x-axis. The area swept out by a polar curve r = f(θ) as θ ranges from α to β is A = (1/2)∫ [r(θ)]² dθ. This formula comes from treating each sector as a thin triangle with area (1/2)r² dθ.

Common polar curves include circles (r = a), cardioids (r = a(1 + cosθ)), limaçons (r = a + b·cosθ), and rose curves (r = a·cos(nθ)). Rose curves have n petals when n is odd and 2n petals when n is even. To find the area of one petal, trace the curve through the angle range that produces one petal.

The area between two polar curves uses A = (1/2)∫ ([r_outer]² - [r_inner]²) dθ. Be careful with intersections: you may need to find where r₁ = r₂ to determine the correct angular bounds for each region. Unlike rectangular coordinates, a single θ can correspond to overlapping regions.
steps: Sketch the polar curve to identify the region whose area you need.
Determine the angle bounds [α, β] that trace the desired region once.
Set up the integral A = (1/2)∫αᵞ [r(θ)]² dθ.
Evaluate the integral using trigonometric identities (power-reduction formulas).
For area between curves, subtract inner r² from outer r² in the integrand.

examples.title: Area of one petal of r = 4cos(3θ)
examples.text: A rose with n=3 has 3 petals. One petal is traced as θ goes from -π/6 to π/6. A = (1/2)∫₋π/₆ᵞπ/₆ 16cos²(3θ) dθ. Use identity: cos²(3θ) = (1+cos(6θ))/2. A = 4∫ (1+cos(6θ))/2 dθ = 4[θ/2 + sin(6θ)/12] = 4(π/6) = 2π/3. Total area of all 3 petals = 3(2π/3) = 2π.

examples.title: Area inside r = 3sin(θ) (circle)
examples.text: The full circle is traced as θ goes from 0 to π. A = (1/2)∫₀π 9sin²(θ) dθ = (9/2)∫₀π (1-cos(2θ))/2 dθ = (9/4)[θ - sin(2θ)/2]₀π = (9/4)(π) = 9π/4. This equals πr² = π(3/2)² = 9π/4. Consistent with the circle formula.

lessons.tip: Always graph the polar curve first! Many polar curves retrace themselves. For rose curves r = a·cos(nθ), one petal spans from θ = 0 to θ = π/n. Don't integrate over the full [0, 2π] unless you actually want the total area.

quiz.q: The area in polar coordinates is given by:
quiz.explanation: The polar area formula is A = (1/2) ∫αᵞ [r(θ)]² dθ.

quiz.q: How many petals does r = 5sin(4θ) have?
quiz.explanation: When n is even, r = a·sin(nθ) produces 2n = 8 petals.

quiz.q: The area inside r = 2 + 2cos(θ) from θ = 0 to 2π is:
quiz.explanation: This is a cardioid. A = (1/2)∫₀²π (2+2cosθ)² dθ = (1/2)∫(4+8cosθ+4cos²θ)dθ = (1/2)[4(2π)+0+4(π)] = (1/2)(12π) = 6π.

quiz.q: To find the area between two polar curves r₁ and r₂:
quiz.explanation: Area between curves subtracts the inner area from the outer: A = (1/2)∫ (r₁² - r₂²) dθ.

lessons.title: Parametric Curves & Calculus
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of parametric curves & calculus
lessons.formula:
First Derivative (parametric):
  dy/dx = (dy/dt) / (dx/dt)

Second Derivative:
  d²y/dx² = d/dt(dy/dx) / (dx/dt)

Arc Length:
  L = ∫ₐ⁶ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt

Area under parametric curve:
  A = ∫ y(t) · (dx/dt) dt
lessons.content:
Parametric equations define x and y separately as functions of a third variable (the parameter), typically t. Instead of y = f(x), we have x = g(t) and y = h(t). This is especially useful for curves that fail the vertical line test, projectile motion, and paths that loop back on themselves.

To find dy/dx for a parametric curve, apply the chain rule: dy/dx = (dy/dt) / (dx/dt), provided dx/dt ≠ 0. The second derivative d²y/dx² is NOT simply (d²y/dt²)/(d²x/dt²); instead, differentiate dy/dx with respect to t and divide by dx/dt. The curve is concave up where d²y/dx² > 0.

Eliminating the parameter means solving one equation for t and substituting into the other to get a Cartesian equation relating x and y. This helps identify the curve type. The tangent line at parameter t₀ uses the point (g(t₀), h(t₀)) with slope (h'(t₀))/(g'(t₀)).
steps: Write x = g(t) and y = h(t); identify the parameter interval.
Compute dx/dt and dy/dt to find the slope dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).
Find horizontal tangents (dy/dt = 0, dx/dt ≠ 0) and vertical tangents (dx/dt = 0, dy/dt ≠ 0).
For concavity, compute d²y/dx² = [d/dt(dy/dx)] / (dx/dt).
If needed, eliminate t to get a Cartesian equation of the curve.

examples.title: Tangent line to x = t² - 1, y = t³ - t at t = 2
examples.text: Point: x = 3, y = 6. dx/dt = 2t = 4, dy/dt = 3t² - 1 = 11. dy/dx = 11/4. Tangent line: y - 6 = (11/4)(x - 3). d²y/dx² = d/dt(11/(2t)) / (2t) = (-11/(2t²)) / (2t) = -11/(4t³). At t = 2: d²y/dx² = -11/32 < 0, concave down.

examples.title: Eliminate parameter: x = 3cos(t), y = 2sin(t)
examples.text: From x = 3cos(t): cos(t) = x/3. From y = 2sin(t): sin(t) = y/2. Using cos²t + sin²t = 1: (x/3)² + (y/2)² = 1. This is an ellipse centered at the origin with semi-major axis 3 and semi-minor axis 2.

lessons.tip: The most common mistake with parametric derivatives is computing the second derivative. Remember: d²y/dx² ≠ (d²y/dt²)/(d²x/dt²). You must differentiate dy/dx (which is itself a function of t) with respect to t, then divide by dx/dt.

quiz.q: Given x = e^t, y = t², find dy/dx at t = 1.
quiz.explanation: dx/dt = e^t, dy/dt = 2t. dy/dx = 2t/e^t. At t=1: dy/dx = 2/e.

quiz.q: A horizontal tangent occurs when:
options: Both dx/dt and dy/dt are zero
quiz.explanation: Horizontal tangent means slope dy/dx = 0, which requires dy/dt = 0 while dx/dt ≠ 0.

quiz.q: x = 2t + 1, y = t² - 3. What curve is this?
quiz.explanation: Eliminate t: t = (x-1)/2, so y = ((x-1)/2)² - 3 = (x²-2x+1)/4 - 3. This is a parabola.

quiz.q: The second derivative d²y/dx² for parametric curves equals:
quiz.explanation: d²y/dx² = [d/dt(dy/dx)] / (dx/dt). Differentiate the first derivative with respect to t, then divide by dx/dt.

lessons.title: Sequences: Monotonic & Bounded
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of sequences: monotonic & bounded
lessons.formula:
Monotonic: a₁ ≤ a₂ ≤ a₃ ≤ ... (increasing)
          or a₁ ≥ a₂ ≥ a₃ ≥ ... (decreasing)

Bounded above: ∃ M ∈ ℝ such that aₙ ≤ M for all n
Bounded below: ∃ m ∈ ℝ such that aₙ ≥ m for all n

Monotone Convergence Theorem:
  If {aₙ} is bounded AND monotonic, then it converges.
lessons.content:
A sequence is an ordered list of numbers {a₁, a₂, a₃, ...}, written {aₙ}. A sequence is monotonic if its terms either consistently increase (aₙ ≤ aₙ+₁ for all n, called monotonically increasing) or consistently decrease (aₙ ≥ aₙ+₁ for all n, monotonically decreasing). If inequalities are strict, the sequence is strictly monotonic.

A sequence is bounded above if there exists a real number M such that aₙ ≤ M for all n, and bounded below if aₙ ≥ m for all n. A sequence is simply bounded if it is bounded both above and below. For example, {(-1)^n / n} is bounded (all terms satisfy -1 ≤ aₙ ≤ 1) but not monotonic.

The Monotone Convergence Theorem is a powerful tool: if a sequence is both bounded and monotonic, it must converge to some limit L. This theorem does not tell you what L is, only that it exists. To prove boundedness, you might use induction or find a closed-form expression. To prove monotonicity, show that aₙ+₁ - aₙ has a consistent sign.
steps: Write out several terms to identify a pattern in the sequence.
Check monotonicity: compute aₙ+₁ - aₙ and determine its sign for all n.
Check boundedness: find upper and/or lower bounds for the terms.
If both bounded and monotonic, apply the Monotone Convergence Theorem to conclude convergence.
To find the actual limit L, solve L = f(L) if aₙ+₁ = f(aₙ) for a recursive sequence.

examples.title: Is {n/(n+1)} monotonic and bounded?
examples.text: aₙ = n/(n+1). Difference: aₙ+₁ - aₙ = (n+1)/(n+2) - n/(n+1) = 1/((n+1)(n+2)) > 0. Increasing (monotonic). Bounded: 0 < n/(n+1) < 1 for all n. By the MCT, it converges. The limit is lim(n/(n+1)) = 1.

examples.title: Recursive sequence: a₁ = 1, aₙ+₁ = √(6 + aₙ)
examples.text: a₁ = 1, a₂ = √7 ≈ 2.65, a₃ = √(6+√7) ≈ 2.91, a₄ ≈ 2.98. The sequence appears increasing. If bounded by 3: assume aₙ < 3, then aₙ+₁ = √(6+aₙ) < √9 = 3. Bounded above by 3 and increasing → converges by MCT. Find L: L = √(6+L) → L² = 6+L → L² - L - 6 = 0 → L = 3 (taking positive root).

lessons.tip: For recursive sequences aₙ+₁ = f(aₙ), you can often prove monotonicity and boundedness simultaneously using induction. Assume aₙ is bounded by M and show aₙ+₁ ≤ M. Then assume aₙ < aₙ+₁ and show aₙ+₁ < aₙ+₂.

quiz.q: The Monotone Convergence Theorem states that a sequence converges if it is:
options: Neither bounded nor monotonic but oscillating
quiz.explanation: A sequence is guaranteed to converge if and only if it is both bounded AND monotonic.

quiz.q: The sequence {(-1)^n} is:
quiz.explanation: {(-1)^n} alternates: -1, 1, -1, 1, ... It is bounded (all terms in [-1, 1]) but not monotonic (it alternates).

quiz.q: The sequence {2^n} is:
quiz.explanation: {2^n} = 2, 4, 8, 16, ... is strictly increasing (monotonic) but has no upper bound, so it diverges.

quiz.q: Prove aₙ = (2n+1)/(n+1) is monotonic. What is aₙ+₁ - aₙ?

lessons.title: Integral Test & p-Series
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of integral test & p-series
lessons.formula:
Integral Test:
  If f is positive, continuous, and decreasing on [1, ∞),
  then Σ aₙ converges ⇔ ∫₁∞ f(x) dx converges
  where aₙ = f(n)

p-Series: Σ 1/n⁶
  Converges if p > 1, Diverges if p ≤ 1

Harmonic series: Σ 1/n diverges (p = 1 case)

Remainder estimate: Rₙ ≤ ∫ₙ∞ f(x) dx
lessons.content:
The Integral Test connects the convergence of an infinite series to the convergence of an improper integral. If f is a positive, continuous, decreasing function on [1, ∞) and aₙ = f(n), then the series Σ aₙ converges if and only if the improper integral ∫₁∞ f(x) dx converges. This test applies to series where the terms can be expressed as a function of n that is nice enough to integrate.

A p-series has the form Σₙ=₁∞ 1/n⁶. It converges when p > 1 and diverges when p ≤ 1. The most famous special case is the harmonic series Σ 1/n (p = 1), which diverges even though its terms approach zero. This counterintuitive result is proved by the integral test: ∫ 1/x dx = ln(x), which diverges as x → ∞.

The Integral Test also gives a remainder estimate: if you approximate the sum of a convergent series by the first n terms, the error Rₙ satisfies Rₙ ≤ ∫ₙ∞ f(x) dx. This bounds how far off your partial sum is from the true infinite sum. For example, using 10 terms of the harmonic series remainder gives R₁₀ ≤ ∫₁₀∞ 1/x dx = ln(∞) - ln(10), which is infinite (confirming divergence).
steps: Verify the function f(n) = aₙ is positive, continuous, and decreasing on [N, ∞).
Set up the corresponding improper integral ∫ₙ∞ f(x) dx.
Evaluate the improper integral using limits.
If the integral converges to a finite value, the series converges. If it diverges, so does the series.
For p-series, simply check: does p > 1? If yes, converges; otherwise, diverges.

examples.title: Does Σ 1/(n² + 1) converge?
examples.text: f(x) = 1/(x²+1) is positive, continuous, decreasing for x ≥ 1. ∫₁∞ 1/(x²+1) dx = [arctan(x)]₁∞ = π/2 - π/4 = π/4. The integral converges, so the series Σ 1/(n²+1) also converges.

examples.title: p-Series: Σ 1/n³ (converges) vs Σ 1/√n (diverges)
examples.text: Σ 1/n³: p = 3 > 1, so it converges. ∫ 1/x³ dx = -1/(2x²), finite as x → ∞. Σ 1/√n = Σ 1/n^(1/2): p = 1/2 ≤ 1, so it diverges. ∫ 1/x^(1/2) dx = 2x^(1/2), which diverges as x → ∞.

lessons.tip: The Integral Test tells you WHETHER a series converges, not WHAT it converges to. To find the actual sum, you typically need a different method. Also, always verify the function is decreasing (f'(x) < 0) before applying the test.

quiz.q: Does the p-series Σ 1/n⁴ converge?
options: No, because the terms are too large
quiz.explanation: A p-series Σ 1/n⁶ converges if and only if p > 1. Here p = 4 > 1, so it converges.

quiz.q: The harmonic series Σ 1/n is surprising because:
options: It converges to a large number
quiz.explanation: The harmonic series diverges (p = 1 ≤ 1), which is counterintuitive because terms go to zero. Going to zero is necessary but not sufficient for convergence.

quiz.q: Before applying the Integral Test, you must verify f is:
quiz.explanation: All three conditions are required: f positive, continuous, and decreasing on [N, ∞).

quiz.q: The remainder estimate Rₙ ≤ ∫ₙ∞ f(x) dx tells us:
options: The exact sum of the series
An upper bound on the error when using n terms to approximate the sum
The value of the nth term
Whether the series converges or diverges
quiz.explanation: Rₙ bounds the tail of the series — the difference between the partial sum Sₙ and the true sum S. It quantifies the approximation error.

lessons.title: Comparison Tests (Direct & Limit)
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of comparison tests (direct & limit)
lessons.formula:
Direct Comparison Test (DCT):
If 0 <= a_n <= b_n for all n, then:
  - If sum(b_n) converges, then sum(a_n) converges
  - If sum(a_n) diverges, then sum(b_n) diverges

Limit Comparison Test (LCT):
Let L = lim(n->inf) a_n / b_n
  - If 0 < L < inf, both series behave the same
  - If L = 0 and sum(b_n) converges, sum(a_n) converges
  - If L = inf and sum(b_n) diverges, sum(a_n) diverges

p-series: sum(1/n^p)
  Converges if p > 1, diverges if p <= 1
lessons.content:
When you encounter an unfamiliar infinite series, the comparison tests let you determine convergence by comparing it to a series you already know. The Direct Comparison Test requires a term-by-term inequality: if every term of your series is smaller than the corresponding term of a convergent series, your series also converges. Conversely, if your series' terms dominate a divergent series, your series diverges too.

The Limit Comparison Test is often more flexible. Instead of requiring a strict inequality for every term, you compute the limit of the ratio a_n/b_n as n approaches infinity. If the limit is a positive finite number (0 < L < infinity), then both series either converge or diverge together. This is incredibly powerful because you only need to check the limiting behaviour of the terms, not every single term.

Both tests rely on having a good benchmark series ready — usually a p-series (1/n^p) or a geometric series. Choosing the right benchmark is often the hardest part. Start by identifying the dominant term in a_n for large n, then pick a p-series that matches that growth rate.
steps: Identify the dominant behaviour of a_n as n grows large (e.g., 1/n^2, 1/(n ln n))
Choose a benchmark series b_n whose terms have the same dominant behaviour
Check the sign condition: both a_n and b_n must be positive for large n
Apply the LCT: compute L = lim(a_n / b_n)
Interpret: if 0 < L < inf, both series share the same convergence result; then verify with the DCT inequality if needed

examples.title: Limit Comparison Test: sum(1/(n^2 + 3))
examples.text: Compare with b_n = 1/n^2 (a convergent p-series, p=2>1). L = lim(n->inf) [1/(n^2+3)] / [1/n^2] = lim(n->inf) n^2/(n^2+3) = 1. Since 0 < 1 < inf, both series behave the same. Because sum(1/n^2) converges, sum(1/(n^2+3)) also converges.

examples.title: Direct Comparison Test: sum(1/(2^n + n))
examples.text: For all n>=1: 0 < 1/(2^n + n) < 1/2^n. The geometric series sum(1/2^n) converges (ratio=1/2 < 1). By the DCT, since each term of our series is smaller than a convergent series' term, sum(1/(2^n + n)) converges.

lessons.tip: When choosing a benchmark for the Limit Comparison Test, drop lower-order terms first. For a_n = (3n+1)/(n^3-2), the dominant behaviour is 3n/n^3 = 3/n^2, so compare with b_n = 1/n^2. The constant factor cancels out in the limit!

quiz.q: To use the Limit Comparison Test, what must be true about a_n and b_n for large n?
options: They must be positive (or eventually positive)
quiz.explanation: Both a_n and b_n must be positive (or eventually positive) so that the limit of their ratio is meaningful and the comparison logic holds.

quiz.q: If lim(a_n/b_n) = 1/2, what does the LCT tell you?
options: Both series converge or both diverge
quiz.explanation: When L is a positive finite number (0 < L < infinity), both series share the same convergence behaviour.

quiz.q: The p-series sum(1/n^p) converges when p > 1. Does sum(1/(n^1.5)) converge?
options: It depends on the starting index
quiz.explanation: A p-series converges whenever p > 1. Since 1.5 > 1, the series converges.

quiz.q: Using the DCT, if 0 <= a_n <= b_n and sum(a_n) diverges, what can you conclude about sum(b_n)?
quiz.explanation: If the smaller series diverges, the larger series must also diverge — you cannot 'save' a divergent series by making its terms bigger.

lessons.title: Ratio & Root Tests
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of ratio & root tests
lessons.formula:
Ratio Test:
L = lim(n->inf) |a_{n+1} / a_n|
  L < 1  => converges absolutely
  L > 1  => diverges
  L = 1  => inconclusive

Root Test:
L = lim(n->inf) |a_n|^(1/n)
  L < 1  => converges absolutely
  L > 1  => diverges
  L = 1  => inconclusive
lessons.content:
The Ratio Test and Root Test are two of the most versatile convergence tests. They work especially well when the terms of a series involve factorials (n!), exponentials (c^n), or products where the ratio of consecutive terms simplifies nicely.

The Ratio Test computes the limit of the absolute value of a_{n+1}/a_n. If this limit L is strictly less than 1, the series converges absolutely (meaning even the series of absolute values converges). If L > 1, the series diverges because the terms are actually growing. If L = 1, the test is inconclusive — the series might converge or diverge.

The Root Test takes the nth root of |a_n| and evaluates the limit. It is especially powerful when terms are raised to the nth power, such as in series like sum((n/(2n+1))^n). The decision rule is the same: L < 1 converges, L > 1 diverges, L = 1 is inconclusive. The Root Test and Ratio Test always agree when both produce a definitive answer.
steps: Write out the general term a_n of the series
For the Ratio Test: form the ratio |a_{n+1}/a_n| and simplify
Take the limit as n approaches infinity
If L < 1, the series converges absolutely; if L > 1, it diverges
If L = 1 (Ratio Test inconclusive), try the Root Test or another test

examples.title: Ratio Test: sum(n! / 10^n)
examples.text: a_n = n!/10^n. Ratio: |a_{n+1}/a_n| = [(n+1)!/10^(n+1)] / [n!/10^n] = (n+1)/10. Limit = lim(n+1)/10 = infinity. Since L = infinity > 1, the series diverges. The factorial grows much faster than 10^n.

examples.title: Root Test: sum((n/(3n+1))^n)
examples.text: a_n = (n/(3n+1))^n. Root: |a_n|^(1/n) = n/(3n+1). Limit = lim n/(3n+1) = 1/3. Since L = 1/3 < 1, the series converges absolutely.

lessons.tip: Use the Ratio Test when the general term involves factorials (n!) or exponentials (c^n) because consecutive ratios cancel beautifully. Use the Root Test when the nth power appears in the term itself — the nth root simply removes it!

quiz.q: If the Ratio Test gives L = 0.75, what do you conclude?
quiz.explanation: L = 0.75 < 1, so the series converges absolutely.

quiz.q: When the Ratio Test gives L = 1, what should you do?
options: Try a different test (Root, Comparison, Integral, etc.)
Give up — the problem is unsolvable
quiz.explanation: L = 1 is inconclusive for the Ratio Test. You must try another convergence test.

quiz.q: Which test is best for sum(n!/5^n)?
quiz.explanation: The Ratio Test is ideal here because factorials cancel neatly in consecutive ratios: (n+1)!/n! = n+1.

quiz.q: The Root Test and Ratio Test always agree when:
quiz.explanation: When both tests yield a definitive answer (L != 1), they always agree on convergence or divergence.

lessons.title: Alternating Series & Absolute Convergence
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of alternating series & absolute convergence
lessons.formula:
Alternating Series Test:
sum((-1)^(n-1) * b_n) converges if:
  1) b_n >= 0 for all n
  2) b_{n+1} <= b_n (eventually decreasing)
  3) lim(n->inf) b_n = 0

Absolute Convergence:
If sum|a_n| converges => sum(a_n) converges absolutely
If sum|a_n| diverges but sum(a_n) converges => conditional

Remainder estimate: |R_n| <= b_{n+1}
lessons.content:
An alternating series has terms that switch sign in a regular pattern, typically using (-1)^n. The Alternating Series Test (also called the Leibniz Test) gives conditions under which such a series converges: the absolute values of the terms must be decreasing and must approach zero.

Convergence of an alternating series can be absolute or conditional. A series converges absolutely if the series of absolute values converges (check with Ratio, Root, or Comparison tests). If the original alternating series converges but the series of absolute values diverges, the convergence is conditional — the series only converges because the sign changes cause cancellation.

A beautiful feature of convergent alternating series is the remainder estimate: if you stop after n terms, the error is at most the size of the very next term. This makes alternating series excellent for numerical approximation.
steps: Identify the alternating sign pattern and the positive term sequence b_n
Verify that b_n is (eventually) decreasing: check b_{n+1} <= b_n
Verify that lim(b_n) = 0
If conditions 2 and 3 hold, the alternating series converges
Test sum(|a_n|) to determine whether convergence is absolute or conditional

examples.title: Alternating Harmonic Series: sum((-1)^(n+1)/n)
examples.text: b_n = 1/n. Check: (1) 1/n > 0. (2) 1/(n+1) <= 1/n — decreasing. (3) lim(1/n) = 0. All conditions satisfied — the series converges. But sum(1/n) diverges (harmonic series). So convergence is CONDITIONAL, not absolute. The partial sum S_10 approximates ln(2) with error |R_10| <= 1/11.

examples.title: Absolute Convergence: sum((-1)^n / n^2)
examples.text: The alternating series converges by the AST (b_n=1/n^2 decreases to 0). Now check sum(1/n^2): this is a p-series with p=2>1, so it converges. Since sum(|a_n|) = sum(1/n^2) converges, the original series converges ABSOLUTELY.

lessons.tip: Remember: absolute convergence is STRONGER than conditional convergence. An absolutely convergent series can be rearranged in any order and still converge to the same sum. A conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to converge to ANY value — or even diverge!

quiz.q: Which condition is NOT required by the Alternating Series Test?
quiz.explanation: The AST only requires the three listed conditions. The series sum(b_n) does NOT need to converge — only the alternating version sum((-1)^n b_n) converges.

quiz.q: A series converges conditionally when:
options: Both the series and its absolute-value version converge
The series converges but sum|a_n| diverges
The series diverges but sum|a_n| converges
Both the series and its absolute-value version diverge
quiz.explanation: Conditional convergence means the alternating series converges, but the series of absolute values diverges.

quiz.q: For a convergent alternating series, the error after n terms is at most:
options: The sum of all remaining terms
quiz.explanation: The Alternating Series Remainder Theorem states |R_n| <= b_{n+1} — the error is bounded by the first omitted term.

quiz.q: Does sum((-1)^n / n^3) converge absolutely?
options: Yes, because sum(1/n^3) is a convergent p-series (p=3>1)
quiz.explanation: sum(|(-1)^n / n^3|) = sum(1/n^3) which is a p-series with p=3>1, so it converges. The original series converges absolutely.

lessons.title: Power Series & Radius of Convergence
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of power series & radius of convergence
lessons.formula:
Power Series: sum(c_n * (x - a)^n), n=0 to inf
a = center of the series
c_n = coefficients

Radius of Convergence (via Ratio Test):
R = lim(n->inf) |c_n / c_{n+1}|
or: 1/R = lim(n->inf) |c_{n+1}/c_n|^{1/n}

Interval of Convergence: (a - R, a + R)
Test endpoints separately!
lessons.content:
A power series is an infinite series of the form sum(c_n (x − a)^n) where c_n are coefficients and a is the center. Unlike the numerical series you have studied (which produce a single number), a power series defines a function of x. For some values of x it converges, for others it diverges. The set of x-values where the series converges is called the interval of convergence.

The Radius of Convergence R determines how far from the center the series converges. The series converges absolutely for all x with |x − a| < R, diverges for |x − a| > R, and may or may not converge at the endpoints x = a ± R. The endpoints must be tested individually — sometimes you get a convergent p-series or alternating series at an endpoint.

To find R, apply the Ratio Test to the absolute value of the general term, treating x as a variable. The inequality |x − a| < R emerges directly from requiring the ratio limit to be less than 1. Three special cases: R = 0 (converges only at x = a), R = infinity (converges for all x), and 0 < R < infinity (converges on a finite interval).
steps: Identify the general term c_n (x - a)^n and note the center a
Apply the Ratio Test: compute lim |c_{n+1}(x-a)^{n+1} / c_n(x-a)^n|
Simplify to isolate |x - a| times a limit involving only the coefficients
Set the expression < 1 and solve for |x - a| to get R
Test convergence at x = a - R and x = a + R individually using other tests

examples.title: Finding R: sum(x^n / n!)
examples.text: a_n = x^n / n!. Ratio: |a_{n+1}/a_n| = |x^(n+1)/(n+1)!| * n!/|x^n| = |x|/(n+1). Limit = lim |x|/(n+1) = 0 for ALL x. Since L = 0 < 1 for every x, R = infinity. The series converges for all real x (this is the series for e^x).

examples.title: Interval of Convergence: sum((x-2)^n / n)
examples.text: Center a = 2. Ratio: |a_{n+1}/a_n| = |(x-2)^(n+1)/(n+1)| * n/|(x-2)^n| = |x-2| * n/(n+1) -> |x-2|. Need |x-2| < 1, so R = 1. Interval: (1, 3). Test endpoints: x=1 gives sum((-1)^n/n), converges by AST (alternating harmonic). x=3 gives sum(1/n), diverges (harmonic). Interval: [1, 3).

lessons.tip: Always test the endpoints! The interval could be (a-R, a+R), [a-R, a+R), (a-R, a+R], or [a-R, a+R]. Missing the endpoints is one of the most common mistakes on calculus exams.

quiz.q: If the Ratio Test for a power series gives L = |x+1|/4, what is the radius of convergence?
quiz.explanation: Set |x+1|/4 < 1, which gives |x+1| < 4. Therefore R = 4.

quiz.q: A power series has center a = 5 and R = 3. Which x-values are at the endpoints?
quiz.explanation: Endpoints are a - R = 5 - 3 = 2 and a + R = 5 + 3 = 8.

quiz.q: If R = 0, the power series converges:
options: Only at the center x = a
quiz.explanation: R = 0 means the series converges only at its center x = a and diverges everywhere else.

quiz.q: After finding the radius of convergence, you must:
options: Accept the result — no further work needed
Test each endpoint individually for convergence
quiz.explanation: Endpoints are always tested separately because the Ratio Test gives L = 1 there, which is inconclusive.

lessons.title: Taylor Polynomials & Error Estimation
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of taylor polynomials & error estimation
lessons.formula:
Taylor Polynomial of degree n centered at a:
P_n(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + f''(a)(x-a)^2/2! + ... + f^(n)(a)(x-a)^n/n!

Lagrange Remainder (Error Bound):
|R_n(x)| <= M * |x-a|^(n+1) / (n+1)!
where M = max|f^(n+1)(z)| for z between a and x

Maclaurin = Taylor centered at a = 0
lessons.content:
A Taylor polynomial approximates a function near a chosen point using the function's derivatives evaluated at that point. The degree-n Taylor polynomial P_n(x) matches the function's value, slope, curvature, and higher-order behaviours at the center up to the nth derivative. A Maclaurin polynomial is simply a Taylor polynomial centered at zero.

The Lagrange Remainder Theorem gives a rigorous error bound. If |f^(n+1)(z)| is bounded by M for all z between the center a and the point x, then the error |f(x) − P_n(x)| is at most M|x − a|^(n+1)/(n+1)!. This is crucial for determining how many terms you need to achieve a desired accuracy.

Higher-degree polynomials give better approximations over a wider range, but each additional term requires computing another derivative. For many standard functions (sin x, e^x, ln(1+x)), the Taylor polynomials have well-known patterns that make them easy to write without computing derivatives individually each time.
steps: Choose the center a and the desired degree n
Compute f(a), f'(a), f''(a), ..., f^(n)(a)
Write P_n(x) = sum of f^(k)(a)*(x-a)^k / k! for k = 0 to n
For error estimation: find an upper bound M on |f^(n+1)(z)| in the interval
Apply Lagrange formula: error <= M*|x-a|^(n+1)/(n+1)!

examples.title: Lagrange Error Bound for sin(x) at x = 0.3
examples.text: Use P_3(x) = x - x^3/6. Need error bound for f^(4)(z) = sin(z). Max |sin(z)| = 1 for all z. M = 1, |x-0| = 0.3, n+1 = 4. Error <= 1 * 0.3^4 / 4! = 0.0081/24 = 0.0003375. So P_3(0.3) approximates sin(0.3) to within 0.00034.

lessons.tip: For sin(x) and cos(x) centered at 0, the derivatives cycle through sin, cos, -sin, -cos repeatedly. You can write out many terms without computing each derivative from scratch. Also, sin(x) is an odd function so its Maclaurin series has only odd-powered terms!

quiz.q: What is the Maclaurin polynomial of degree 2 for f(x) = cos(x)?
The Lagrange remainder uses the (n+1)th derivative because:
options: It looks better in the formula
The nth-degree polynomial uses derivatives up to order n, so the next unused derivative controls the error
The nth derivative is always zero
There is no reason — it is arbitrary
quiz.explanation: P_n uses derivatives f through f^(n). The remaining error is governed by f^(n+1), the next higher derivative not included in the polynomial.

quiz.q: A Maclaurin polynomial is a Taylor polynomial centered at:
quiz.explanation: Maclaurin polynomials are Taylor polynomials with center a = 0.

quiz.q: To guarantee an approximation error of less than 0.001, you should:
options: Use the Lagrange error bound to find the minimum degree needed
quiz.explanation: The Lagrange remainder theorem lets you calculate the exact degree required so that the error bound is below your tolerance.

lessons.title: Surface Area of Revolution
lessons.description: Calculate surface area generated by revolving a curve around an axis.

SA = 2π ∫ r · ds
Around x-axis: SA = 2π∫y·√(1+(dy/dx)²)dx
Around y-axis: SA = 2π∫x·√(1+(dy/dx)²)dx

Determine radius (y for x-axis, x for y-axis)
Compute dy/dx and set up integrand
Evaluate the integral

lessons.title: Integration by Parts
lessons.description: Integrate products of functions using the Integration by Parts formula.
lessons.formula:
Integration by Parts Formula:
∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du

Derived from the Product Rule:
d(uv) = u dv + v du  →  ∫(u dv + v du) = uv

LIATE Rule (choose u in this priority):
  L – Logarithmic functions (ln x)
  I – Inverse trig (arctan x, arcsin x)
  A – Algebraic functions (xⁿ, polynomials)
  T – Trig functions (sin x, cos x)
  E – Exponential functions (eˣ)

Tabular Method (for repeated IBP):
Differentiate u column, integrate dv column, alternate signs +, −, +, −...
lessons.content:
Integration by Parts is a technique for evaluating integrals of products of functions that cannot be simplified by substitution alone. The formula ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du is derived directly from the product rule for differentiation. To apply it, you choose which part of the integrand is u and which is dv, then compute du and v, and substitute into the formula. The key challenge is making a good choice for u — choosing wisely can turn a difficult integral into a simpler one.

The LIATE rule provides a reliable guide for choosing u. You should select u from the function type that appears highest in the LIATE priority list: Logarithmic first, then Inverse trigonometric, Algebraic, Trigonometric, and Exponential last. For example, in ∫ x·eˣ dx, choose u = x (algebraic, higher priority than exponential) and dv = eˣ dx. When one factor is a polynomial and you need to apply integration by parts repeatedly, the tabular method (also called the DI method) dramatically speeds up the process by organizing repeated differentiation and integration into a compact table.

Mastery of integration by parts opens the door to evaluating a wide variety of important integrals, including those involving logarithmic and inverse trigonometric functions. It is also the foundation for reduction formulas, which express an integral in terms of another integral of the same type with a lower exponent, making previously intractable problems tractable through recursion.
steps: Identify the two components of the integrand and apply the LIATE rule to choose u (the factor higher in LIATE priority) and dv (everything else).
Compute du by differentiating u, and find v by integrating dv.
Substitute u, v, du into the Integration by Parts formula: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du.
Evaluate the remaining integral ∫ v du — if it requires integration by parts again, repeat the process or use the tabular method.
Simplify the final expression and add the constant of integration C.

examples.title: ∫ x·cos(x) dx
examples.text: Let u = x → du = dx. Let dv = cos(x) dx → v = sin(x). Apply the formula: ∫ x cos(x) dx = x sin(x) − ∫ sin(x) dx = x sin(x) + cos(x) + C. The remaining integral ∫ sin(x) dx is straightforward, giving −cos(x). A single application of IBP was sufficient.

examples.title: ∫ x²·eˣ dx (Tabular Method)
examples.text:
u = x², dv = eˣ dx. Build a table:
Sign | Derivatives of u | Integrals of dv
+    | x²              | eˣ
−   | 2x                | eˣ
+    | 2                 | eˣ
−   | 0 (stop)         | eˣ
Result: +x²·eˣ − 2x·eˣ + 2·eˣ + C = eˣ(x² − 2x + 2) + C. The tabular method handles repeated IBP efficiently without writing each step separately.

lessons.tip: When using the LIATE rule, always check your choice of u and dv before committing. If the remaining integral ∫ v du looks harder than the original, try swapping your choices!

quiz.q: The Integration by Parts formula is derived from which differentiation rule?
quiz.explanation: Integration by Parts comes from the Product Rule: d(uv) = u dv + v du, which integrates to uv = ∫ u dv + ∫ v du.

quiz.q: According to LIATE, for ∫ x·ln(x) dx, u should be:
quiz.explanation: L comes before A in LIATE, so ln(x) (Logarithmic) is chosen as u over x (Algebraic).

quiz.q: In the tabular method, you stop differentiating when:
quiz.explanation: You stop when the derivative column reaches zero OR when the remaining integral is easy to evaluate.

quiz.q: ∫ x·eˣ dx = ?
quiz.explanation: Using IBP with u = x, dv = eˣ dx: ∫ xeˣ dx = xeˣ − ∫ eˣ dx = xeˣ − eˣ + C.

lessons.title: Volume of Solids of Revolution
lessons.description: Calculate volumes using the disk, washer, and shell methods.
lessons.formula:
Disk: V = π∫[f(x)]² dx
Washer: V = π∫([R(x)]²−[r(x)]²) dx
Shell: V = 2π∫x·f(x) dx

Choose method based on axis of rotation!
lessons.content:
The disk/washer method slices a solid perpendicular to the axis of rotation, creating thin disks or washers. Volume = π∫(radius)²dx for disks, or π∫(R²−r²)dx for washers with an inner radius.

The shell method slices parallel to the axis of rotation, creating cylindrical shells. Volume = 2π∫(radius)(height)dx. The shell method is often easier when rotating around a vertical axis.

Choose your method based on which gives simpler integrals. Both always give the same answer!
steps: Sketch the region and identify the axis of rotation
Choose disk/washer (perpendicular to axis) or shell (parallel to axis)
Set up the integral with correct radius and height
Evaluate the definite integral
Include π in the volume formula

examples.title: Disk Method
examples.text: Rotate y=√x from 0 to 4 about x-axis. V=π∫(0→4)(√x)²dx=π∫(0→4)x dx=π[x²/2](0→4)=π(16/2)=8π.

quiz.explanation: Disk: V = π∫(radius)² dx. Simple disk (no hole).

lessons.title: Arc Length & Surface Area
lessons.description: Calculate the length of curves and surface areas of revolution.
lessons.formula:
Arc Length:
L = ∫(a→b) √(1 + [f'(x)]²) dx

Surface Area (about x-axis):
SA = 2π∫(a→b) f(x)√(1+[f'(x)]²) dx
lessons.content:
The arc length of a curve y=f(x) from x=a to x=b is found by integrating the arc length differential: L = ∫√(1+[f'(x)]²)dx. This formula comes from the Pythagorean theorem applied to infinitesimal segments.

The surface area of a surface of revolution combines arc length with circumference: SA = 2π∫f(x)√(1+[f'(x)]²)dx. This is the integral of 2π(radius)(arc length element).
steps: Find f'(x)
Compute 1+[f'(x)]²
Take the square root: √(1+[f'(x)]²)
Set up the definite integral
Evaluate (often requires u-substitution)
lessons.tip: Arc length integrals can be tricky to evaluate analytically. If the integral is too complex, numerical methods are acceptable!

quiz.q: Arc length of y=3x from 0 to 2:
The arc length formula is:
quiz.explanation: L=∫√(1+[f'(x)]²)dx from a to b.

quiz.q: Surface area adds what factor to arc length?
quiz.explanation: SA = 2π(radius)(arc length element) = 2π∫f(x)√(1+[f'(x)]²)dx.

quiz.q: Arc length of y=5 from a to b is:
quiz.explanation: f'(x)=0. L=∫(a→b)√(1+0)dx=b−a. It's a straight horizontal line.

lessons.title: Sequences & Convergence
lessons.description: Understand sequences, limits of sequences, and convergence tests.
lessons.formula:
A sequence converges if lim(n→∞) aₙ = L (finite)
A sequence diverges if the limit is ±∞ or DNE

Squeeze Theorem: if bₙ ≤ aₙ ≤ cₙ and both bₙ,cₙ→L, then aₙ→L
lessons.content:
A sequence is an ordered list of numbers {a₁, a₂, a₃, ...}. We study whether sequences approach a finite limit as n→∞ (convergent) or grow without bound (divergent).

If a sequence converges to L, then for any tolerance ε, eventually all terms are within ε of L. The Squeeze Theorem can prove convergence when the sequence is trapped between two convergent sequences.

Common convergent sequences include 1/n → 0, r^n → 0 (when |r|<1), and n^(1/n) → 1.
steps: Find the general term aₙ
Take the limit as n → ∞
If the limit is a finite number L, the sequence converges
If the limit is ∞, −∞, or DNE, the sequence diverges
Use Squeeze Theorem when direct evaluation is difficult

examples.title: Geometric Sequence
examples.text: aₙ = (2/3)^n. Since |2/3|<1, lim(n→∞)(2/3)^n = 0. The sequence converges to 0.

examples.title: Divergent Sequence
examples.text: aₙ = n/(n+1). lim = 1. Actually this converges! aₙ = n² diverges to ∞.

lessons.tip: Most sequences that converge have their terms getting closer and closer together. If the terms seem to spread out or grow, it likely diverges.

quiz.q: Does aₙ = 1/n converge?
quiz.explanation: lim(n→∞) 1/n = 0. The sequence converges to 0.

quiz.q: Does aₙ = (−1)^n converge?
quiz.explanation: The terms alternate between −1 and 1, never settling to one value. Divergent.

quiz.q: aₙ = (0.5)^n. Limit = ?
The Squeeze Theorem requires:
options: Two bounding sequences with the same limit
quiz.explanation: If bₙ ≤ aₙ ≤ cₙ and both bₙ,cₙ → L, then aₙ → L.

lessons.title: Geometric Series & Telescoping Series
lessons.description: Evaluate geometric and telescoping series.
lessons.formula:
Geometric Series:
Σ(r^n) from n=0 to ∞ = 1/(1−r) when |r|<1

Telescoping: Most terms cancel in the partial sum

Diverges when |r|≥1
lessons.content:
A geometric series is the sum of terms in a geometric sequence: a + ar + ar² + ar³ + ... . It converges to a/(1−r) when |r|<1 and diverges when |r|≥1. This is the most important infinite series formula.

A telescoping series has terms that cancel in pairs when you write out the partial sum. For example: Σ(1/(n(n+1))) telescopes because 1/(n(n+1)) = 1/n − 1/(n+1).
steps: Identify the first term a and common ratio r
Check |r|<1 for convergence
If convergent, sum = a/(1−r)
For telescoping: find the partial sum Sₙ
Cancel terms and take the limit as n→∞
lessons.tip: For geometric series: the formula a/(1−r) gives the sum of a + ar + ar² + ... where 'a' is the FIRST term (not the ratio)!

quiz.q: Σ(0.5)^n from n=0 to ∞ = ?
A geometric series converges when:
quiz.explanation: Geometric series converges if and only if |r| < 1.

quiz.q: Σ2·(−1)^n from n=0 to ∞:
quiz.explanation: r=−1, |r|=1. Geometric series diverges when |r|≥1.

quiz.q: Telescoping series work because:
quiz.explanation: Telescoping series have terms that cancel when the partial sum is expanded.

lessons.title: Taylor & Maclaurin Series
lessons.description: Represent functions as infinite polynomial series.
lessons.formula:
Taylor Series centered at a:
f(x) = Σ f^(n)(a)/n! · (x−a)^n

Maclaurin (a=0):
f(x) = f(0) + f'(0)x + f''(0)x²/2! + ...

Common: e^x = Σx^n/n!, sin x = Σ(−1)^n x^(2n+1)/(2n+1)!
lessons.content:
A Taylor series represents a function as an infinite polynomial: f(x) = Σ f^(n)(a)/n! · (x−a)^n. The Maclaurin series is the special case centered at a=0. These series let us compute function values, integrals, and limits that would otherwise be impossible.

Common Maclaurin series to memorize: e^x = Σx^n/n!, sin x = Σ(−1)^n x^(2n+1)/(2n+1)!, cos x = Σ(−1)^n x^(2n)/(2n)!, ln(1+x) = Σ(−1)^(n+1) x^n/n, and 1/(1−x) = Σx^n.

Every Taylor series has a radius of convergence R — the interval |x−a|
steps: Compute derivatives of f at the center point a
Build the series: Σ f^(n)(a)/n! · (x−a)^n
Find the radius of convergence using the ratio test
Determine convergence at the endpoints
Use the series to approximate function values
lessons.tip: Memorize the 5 common Maclaurin series (e^x, sin, cos, ln(1+x), 1/(1−x)) — they save enormous time on the AP exam and in practice!

quiz.q: Maclaurin series of e^x:
The Maclaurin series is centered at:
quiz.explanation: Maclaurin series are Taylor series centered at a=0.

quiz.q: sin x = Σ(−1)^n x^(2n+1)/(2n+1)! has radius:
quiz.explanation: The Maclaurin series for sin x converges for all real x, so R=∞.

lessons.title: Polar Coordinates
lessons.description: Convert between Cartesian and polar, graph polar equations.
lessons.formula:
x = r cos θ
y = r sin θ
r² = x² + y²
tan θ = y/x

Common polar curves:
Cardioid: r = a(1+cos θ)
Rose: r = a cos(nθ)
lessons.content:
Polar coordinates (r, θ) specify a point by its distance r from the origin (pole) and angle θ from the polar axis. Every point has infinitely many representations: (r, θ) = (r, θ+2kπ) or (−r, θ+π).

Common polar curves include cardioids (heart-shaped, r=a(1±cos θ)), limaçons (r=a±b cos θ), and rose curves (r=a cos(nθ) with n petals when n is odd).

Conversion to/from Cartesian: x=r cos θ, y=r sin θ, r²=x²+y², tan θ=y/x.
steps: Identify the polar equation type
Plot key points at θ=0, π/2, π, 3π/2
Check for symmetry (x-axis, y-axis, origin)
Connect points smoothly
Use r<0 values when needed

examples.title: Cardioid
examples.text: r=1+cos θ. At θ=0: r=2. At θ=π/2: r=1. At θ=π: r=0. Heart-shaped curve symmetric about x-axis.

examples.title: Rose Curve
examples.text: r=2cos(3θ). Has 3 petals (since n=3 is odd). Petals at θ=0, 2π/3, 4π/3.

lessons.tip: For rose curves r=a cos(nθ): n odd → n petals, n even → 2n petals. This is a handy shortcut!

quiz.q: Convert (2, π/3) from polar to Cartesian:
r=1+cos θ is a:
quiz.explanation: r=a(1+cos θ) is the standard cardioid equation.

quiz.q: r=3cos(5θ) has how many petals?
quiz.explanation: n=5 (odd), so the rose has 5 petals.

quiz.q: r²=x²+y² converts from polar to:
quiz.explanation: The conversion from polar to Cartesian gives x²+y²=r².

lessons.title: Parametric Equations
lessons.description: Describe curves using parametric equations and find arc lengths.
lessons.formula:
x = f(t), y = g(t)

dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)

Arc Length:
L = ∫√[(dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²] dt
lessons.content:
Parametric equations describe a curve by giving x and y as functions of a parameter t: x=f(t), y=g(t). This lets us describe curves that fail the vertical line test and model motion in two dimensions.

To find dy/dx for parametric curves: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). The chain rule makes this simple. Second derivatives require the quotient rule applied to (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

Parametric arc length uses the formula L = ∫√[(dx/dt)²+(dy/dt)²]dt, which generalizes the standard arc length formula.
steps: Given x=f(t), y=g(t), identify the parameter interval
Find dx/dt and dy/dt
Compute dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)
For arc length: compute √[(dx/dt)²+(dy/dt)²]
Integrate over the parameter interval

examples.title: Circle
examples.text: x=cos t, y=sin t. dx/dt=−sin t, dy/dt=cos t. dy/dx = cos t/(−sin t) = −cot t. Unit circle traced counterclockwise.

lessons.tip: When a curve would need multiple functions in Cartesian form (like a circle), parametric equations handle it with one pair of equations!

quiz.q: x=cos t, y=sin t traces a:
quiz.explanation: x²+y²=cos²t+sin²t=1. This is the unit circle.

quiz.q: dy/dx for parametric curves = ?
quiz.explanation: By the chain rule: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

quiz.q: The parameter t in parametric equations represents:
quiz.explanation: t is any parameter — often time in physics, but can be any independent variable.

quiz.q: To eliminate the parameter from x=2t, y=t²:
quiz.explanation: t=x/2, so y=(x/2)²=x²/4.

lessons.title: Calculus II Comprehensive Review
lessons.description: Review all Calculus II topics with key formulas and strategies.
lessons.formula:
Key Integration Techniques:
1. u-substitution
2. Integration by parts
3. Trig integrals
4. Partial fractions
5. Improper integrals

Key Series Tests:
Ratio, Root, Comparison, Integral
lessons.content:
Calculus II covers advanced integration techniques (by parts, trig integrals, partial fractions, improper integrals), applications (volumes, arc length, surface area), infinite series (convergence tests, Taylor series), and parametric/polar coordinates.

The most critical skills are: knowing when to apply each integration technique, determining series convergence quickly, and converting between coordinate systems.

For series convergence, use this flowchart: Is it geometric? → check |r|. Is it a p-series? → check p>1. Otherwise → Ratio Test, Comparison Test, or Integral Test.
steps: Review all integration techniques with practice problems
Memorize key Taylor/Maclaurin series
Practice convergence test flowchart
Review polar and parametric conversions
Time yourself on practice exams
