lessons.title: Infinite Series Tests Summary
lessons.description: Compare and apply convergence tests: ratio, root, comparison, integral, alternating
lessons.formula:
Geometric: Σar^n, converges if |r| < 1, sum = a/(1−r)

p-Series: Σ 1/n^p, converges if p > 1

Ratio Test: L = lim |a_(n+1)/a_n|
  L < 1: converges, L > 1: diverges, L = 1: inconclusive

Root Test: L = lim |a_n|^(1/n)
  Same conclusions as ratio test

Alternating Series (Leibniz):
  1. |a_n| decreases
  2. lim a_n = 0
  Both → converges

Comparison: 0 ≤ a_n ≤ b_n,
  if Σb_n converges, so does Σa_n
lessons.content:
An infinite series Σ an converges if the partial sums approach a finite limit. Determining convergence is crucial because a divergent series has no meaningful sum. Different tests apply to different series types, and knowing which to use is a key skill in Calculus II.

The ratio test is best for series with factorials or exponentials. The root test handles nth powers. The comparison test compares to a known series. The integral test works for positive, decreasing functions. The alternating series test (Leibniz criterion) handles series with alternating signs. Start with the divergence test (nth term test): if lim an ≠ 0, the series diverges. This is often the quickest first check.
steps: First: apply the nth term divergence test (lim a_n ≠ 0 → diverges)
For factorials/exponentials: use the ratio test
For nth powers: use the root test
For positive terms resembling known series: use comparison test
For alternating signs: use the alternating series test

examples.title: Ratio Test: Σ n!/3^n
examples.text: a_n = n!/3^n. |a_(n+1)/a_n| = (n+1)!/(3^(n+1)) · 3^n/n! = (n+1)/3. lim(n+1)/3 = ∞. Since L > 1, the series diverges.

examples.title: Alternating Series: Σ (−1)^(n+1)/n²
examples.text: a_n = 1/n²: decreases and → 0. By alternating series test, converges. Also converges absolutely (p-series with p=2 > 1). Sum converges to π²/12.

lessons.tip: Test hierarchy: 1) Divergence test (quick check), 2) Geometric/p-series (recognize patterns), 3) Ratio/root test (factorials, exponentials, nth powers), 4) Comparison/integral test (positive terms), 5) Alternating series test. Start simple, escalate as needed!

quiz.q: Does Σ 1/n diverge or converge?
quiz.explanation: This is the harmonic series (p-series with p=1). Since p = 1 ≤ 1, it diverges. Classic counterexample to 'terms going to 0 means convergence.'

quiz.q: The ratio test is inconclusive when L equals what?
quiz.explanation: When L = 1, the ratio test gives no information. You must try a different test.

quiz.q: For alternating series, what two conditions guarantee convergence?
quiz.explanation: The alternating series test requires: (1) |a_n| decreases, and (2) lim a_n = 0.

lessons.title: Fourier Series
lessons.description: Understand Fourier series representation and compute coefficients
lessons.formula:
Fourier Series:
f(x) = a₀/2 + Σ[a_n cos(nπx/L) + b_n sin(nπx/L)]

Coefficients:
a₀ = (1/L) ∫[−L to L] f(x) dx
a_n = (1/L) ∫[−L to L] f(x) cos(nπx/L) dx
b_n = (1/L) ∫[−L to L] f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx

Period: 2L

Only a_n terms for even functions
Only b_n terms for odd functions
lessons.content:
A Fourier series represents a periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines. Any reasonable periodic function f(x) with period 2L can be written as an infinite series of sine and cosine terms with specific Fourier coefficients. This remarkable result shows that complex waveforms are built from simple harmonic components.

The an coefficients multiply cosine terms and bn coefficients multiply sine terms. For even functions (symmetric about y-axis), only cosine terms appear. For odd functions (symmetric about origin), only sine terms appear. Fourier series converge to f(x) at points of continuity, and to the average of the left and right limits at jump discontinuities. Applications include signal processing, heat conduction, sound analysis, and image compression.
steps: Determine the period 2L of the function
Compute a₀ = (1/L) ∫ f(x) dx over one period
Compute a_n = (1/L) ∫ f(x)cos(nπx/L) dx for each n
Compute b_n = (1/L) ∫ f(x)sin(nπx/L) dx for each n
Write the Fourier series with the computed coefficients

examples.title: Square Wave Fourier Series
examples.text: f(x) = 1 for 0 < x < π, f(x) = −1 for −π < x < 0 (odd function, period 2π). Since odd: all a_n = 0. b_n = (2/π)∫[0 to π] sin(nx) dx = (2/nπ)(1−cos(nπ)) = {4/nπ if n odd, 0 if n even}. f(x) = (4/π)[sin(x) + sin(3x)/3 + sin(5x)/5 + ...].

examples.title: Computing a₀ for a Constant
examples.text: f(x) = 3 on [−π, π]. a₀ = (1/π)∫[−π to π] 3 dx = (1/π)[6π] = 6. a₀/2 = 3. The Fourier series of a constant is just the constant itself (all other coefficients = 0).

lessons.tip: Even/odd symmetry saves tons of work! If f(x) is even (f(−x) = f(x)), all b_n = 0. If f(x) is odd (f(−x) = −f(x)), all a_n = 0 and a₀ = 0. Always check symmetry before computing integrals!

quiz.q: What does a Fourier series represent?
options: A periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines
quiz.explanation: A Fourier series represents any periodic function as a sum of sine and cosine terms (harmonics).

quiz.q: For an odd function, which coefficients are zero?
quiz.explanation: For odd functions: all a_n = 0 and a₀ = 0 (since the integrand f(x)cos(nπx/L) is odd, its integral over a symmetric interval is zero).

quiz.q: The fundamental frequency of a Fourier series corresponds to which n value?
quiz.explanation: The n = 1 term gives the fundamental frequency. Higher n values give harmonics (integer multiples).

lessons.title: Vector-Valued Functions
lessons.description: Analyze vector-valued functions, find derivatives and integrals
lessons.formula:
Vector-Valued Function:
r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t), z(t)⟩

Derivative:
r'(t) = ⟨x'(t), y'(t), z'(t)⟩
(tangent vector)

Speed:
|r'(t)| = √(x'² + y'² + z'²)

Unit Tangent Vector:
T(t) = r'(t)/|r'(t)|

Integral:
∫ r(t) dt = ⟨∫x(t)dt, ∫y(t)dt, ∫z(t)dt⟩ + C
lessons.content:
A vector-valued function r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t), z(t)⟩ maps a parameter t to a point (or vector) in 2D or 3D space. As t varies, the tip of the vector traces a parametric curve (or space curve in 3D). Differentiation and integration work component-by-component, just like scalar functions.

The derivative r'(t) = ⟨x'(t), y'(t), z'(t)⟩ is the tangent vector—it points in the direction the curve is moving at time t. Its magnitude |r'(t)| is the speed. The unit tangent vector T(t) = r'(t)/|r'(t)| always has length 1. Integrating a vector-valued function gives the position function when you start from the velocity function, or vice versa. Applications include projectile motion in 3D, planetary orbits, and particle physics.
steps: Write the vector-valued function r(t) in component form
Differentiate each component separately to find r'(t)
Find the speed: |r'(t)| = √ of sum of squared components
Find the unit tangent: T(t) = r'(t)/|r'(t)|
Integrate each component to find position or displacement

examples.title: Helix Analysis
examples.text: r(t) = ⟨2cos(t), 2sin(t), t⟩. r'(t) = ⟨−2sin(t), 2cos(t), 1⟩. Speed = √(4sin²t + 4cos²t + 1) = √(4+1) = √5. T(t) = ⟨−2sin(t), 2cos(t), 1⟩/√5. Constant speed helix!

lessons.tip: Vector-valued calculus is just component-by-component calculus! Differentiate and integrate each component separately. The only tricky part is remembering that r'(t) gives the tangent VECTOR (with direction), while |r'(t)| gives the SCALAR speed.

quiz.q: r(t) = ⟨t², 2t⟩. What is r'(1)?
The speed is the magnitude of which vector?
quiz.explanation: Speed = |r'(t)|, the magnitude of the velocity (tangent) vector.

quiz.q: How do you integrate r(t) = ⟨cos t, sin t⟩?
quiz.explanation: ∫ cos t dt = sin t, ∫ sin t dt = −cos t. r(t) dt = ⟨sin t, −cos t⟩ + C.

lessons.title: Parametric Arc Length
lessons.description: Calculate arc length of parametric curves
lessons.formula:
Arc Length (Parametric):
L = ∫[a to b] √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt

In 3D:
L = ∫[a to b] ∪((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)² + (dz/dt)²) dt

Differential Arc Length:
ds = √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt

Speed = ds/dt = |r'(t)|
lessons.content:
The arc length of a parametric curve x = f(t), y = g(t) from t = a to t = b is the total distance traveled along the curve. The formula L = ∫ √((dx/dt)2 + (dy/dt)2) dt essentially adds up infinitesimal straight-line segments along the curve. For 3D curves, add the (dz/dt)2 term under the radical.

A curve is smooth if both dx/dt and dy/dt are continuous and not simultaneously zero. The arc length integral can be difficult to evaluate analytically—many common curves have integrals with no elementary antiderivative. In such cases, numerical methods (like Simpson's rule) are used. Note: arc length is always positive (it's a distance), and it depends on the parameterization but the result is independent of how you parametrize the curve.
steps: Find dx/dt and dy/dt by differentiating x(t) and y(t)
Set up the integral: L = ∫ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt
Determine the limits of integration (parameter values for start and end)
Evaluate the integral (often requires numerical methods)
The result is the total arc length in the same units as x and y

examples.title: Arc Length of a Semicircle
examples.text: x = 3cos(t), y = 3sin(t) from t = 0 to t = π. dx/dt = −3sin(t), dy/dt = 3cos(t). L = ∫[0 to π] √(9sin²t+9cos²t) dt = ∫[0 to π] 3 dt = 3π. Half the circumference of a circle of radius 3.

lessons.tip: The arc length integral often leads to integrals of √(1 + [f'(x)]²) or √([f'(t)]² + [g'(t)]²). These are notoriously hard to integrate! Practice with trigonometric substitution. When you can't integrate analytically, use a calculator or numerical method.

quiz.q: What is the arc length of x = cos(t), y = sin(t) from t = 0 to 2π?
quiz.explanation: dx/dt = −sin(t), dy/dt = cos(t). L = ∫[0 to 2π] √(sin²t+cos²t) dt = ∫ 1 dt = 2π. Full circumference.

quiz.q: The arc length formula for parametric curves involves...
quiz.explanation: L = ∫ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt integrates the speed of the parametric motion.

quiz.q: Arc length is always...
quiz.explanation: Arc length represents a physical distance, which is always non-negative.

lessons.title: Differential Equations Applications
lessons.description: Model and solve real-world differential equations (population, mixing, cooling)
lessons.formula:
Newton's Law of Cooling:
dT/dt = −k(T − T_env)
Solution: T(t) = T_env + (T₀ − T_env)e^(−kt)

Mixing Problem:
dA/dt = rate_in − rate_out
  = c_in · r_in − (A(t)/V) · r_out

Population with Carrying Capacity:
dP/dt = kP(1 − P/K)

Falling Body (with air resistance):
dv/dt = g − (k/m)v
lessons.content:
Differential equations model how quantities change over time. Newton's Law of Cooling states that the rate of temperature change is proportional to the difference between the object's temperature and the environment. Mixing problems track the concentration of a substance in a tank as fluid flows in and out.

Population models include exponential growth (dP/dt = kP) and logistic growth (dP/dt = kP(1 − P/K)). Falling body problems with air resistance lead to terminal velocity solutions. Each scenario requires: identifying the rate of change, writing the differential equation, solving it (often by separation of variables), and applying initial conditions. The solutions give predictive models for real-world phenomena.
steps: Identify the quantity changing and what affects its rate of change
Write the differential equation modeling the situation
Identify initial conditions
Solve using separation of variables or other appropriate method
Interpret the solution in the context of the problem

examples.title: Mixing Problem
examples.text: Tank has 100 gal of 50 lb salt. Fresh water enters at 2 gal/min, mixture drains at 2 gal/min. dA/dt = 0 − 2(A/100) = −A/50. A(t) = 50e^(−t/50). After 50 min: A = 50/e ≈ 18.4 lb remain.

lessons.tip: Most applied DEs in this course use separation of variables. The pattern: d(variable)/dt = k × (equilibrium − variable). This always gives exponential approach to equilibrium. The equilibrium solution is where d(variable)/dt = 0, and solutions always approach it asymptotically!

quiz.q: Newton's Law of Cooling: coffee at 95°C in 22°C room. As t → ∞, temperature approaches...
quiz.explanation: As t → ∞, e^(−kt) → 0, so T(t) → T_env = 22°C. The object approaches room temperature.

quiz.q: In a mixing problem, what does dA/dt = rate_in − rate_out represent?
options: Rate of change of amount of substance
quiz.explanation: A(t) represents the amount of substance; dA/dt = (flow in × concentration in) − (flow out × concentration out).

quiz.q: The logistic equation dP/dt = kP(1−P/K) has equilibrium at...
quiz.explanation: Setting dP/dt = 0: kP(1−P/K) = 0 → P = 0 or P = K. Two equilibrium points.

lessons.title: Center of Mass
lessons.description: Calculate center of mass and centroids using integration
lessons.formula:
Center of Mass (1D):
x̄ = (∫ x ρ(x) dx) / (∫ ρ(x) dx)

Centroid of a Region:
x̄ = (1/A) ∫ x · [f(x) − g(x)] dx
ÿ = (1/A) ∫ (1/2)[f(x)² − g(x)²] dx

Where A = ∫ [f(x) − g(x)] dx

For constant density:
centroid = center of mass

Symmetry shortcut:
If region is symmetric about x=a,
then x̄ = a
lessons.content:
The center of mass is the balance point of an object. For a 1D rod with variable density ρ(x), the center of mass x̄ is the weighted average position. For 2D regions (laminas), the centroid (center of mass for uniform density) is found using double integrals or, for regions between curves, single integrals with formulas involving moments.

The x-coordinate of the centroid uses the first moment about the y-axis: the integral of x times the area element. The y-coordinate uses the moment about the x-axis: the integral of (1/2)(f(x)2 − g(x)2). The area A is the integral of (f(x) − g(x)). When density is constant, the centroid is the geometric center. Use symmetry whenever possible: if a region is symmetric about a line, the centroid lies on that line.
steps: Sketch the region and identify the bounding curves f(x) and g(x)
Calculate the total area A = ∫ [f(x) − g(x)] dx
Find x̄ = (1/A) ∫ x[f(x) − g(x)] dx
Find ̏ = (1/A) ∫ (1/2)[f(x)² − g(x)²] dx
Check: if the region has symmetry, the centroid should lie on the axis of symmetry

examples.title: Centroid of a Triangle
examples.text: Triangle with vertices (0,0), (4,0), (0,3). By symmetry: x̄ = (0+4+0)/3 = 4/3, ̏ = (0+0+3)/3 = 1. The centroid of a triangle is always at the intersection of its medians.

examples.title: Centroid of Region Between Curves
examples.text: Region between y = x² and y = 4, x from −2 to 2. Area A = ∫[−2 to 2](4−x²)dx = [4x−x³/3] = 32/3. x̄ = 0 by symmetry. ̏ = (1/A)∫(1/2)(16−x⁴)dx = (3/64)(1/2)(256−128/5) = 8/5.

lessons.tip: Always use symmetry first! If the region is symmetric about x = a, then x̄ = a automatically. If symmetric about y = b, then ̏ = b. This can eliminate half the integration work! Also, the centroid of a triangle is always at the average of the three vertices.

quiz.q: For a uniform semicircle of radius r, where is the centroid?
quiz.explanation: The centroid of a semicircular region lies along the axis of symmetry at distance 4r/(3π) from the center (diameter).

quiz.q: If a region is symmetric about the y-axis, what is x̄?
quiz.explanation: By symmetry about the y-axis, the centroid lies on the y-axis, so x̄ = 0.

quiz.q: The centroid is the same as the center of mass when...
quiz.explanation: The centroid (geometric center) equals the center of mass when density is uniform (constant throughout the object).
